comment: Rules for `node scripts/test.js --changed`: the plans a change runs. Both kinds are applied to every changed file. A directory rule (`directoryRules`) looks the path up under test/plans/feat and names the deepest plan directory or plan file that mirrors it (modules/tensor/ops.cpp -> feat/modules/tensor, test/cases/compile/enum/x.cml -> feat/compile/enum.plan.toml). A file rule (`rules`) then adds the plans outside that mirrored tree that the same change can also break (modules/tiles -> test/plans/gpu/tiles*, modules/onnx -> the exporter in feat/trans); the first matching file rule applies to a file, so keep them from specific to general. A rule entry is a path under test/plans, { "plan": path, "layer": true } or { "plan": path, "ownCases": true }: an ownCases plan is added only when the changed file is one of the `case` paths it names, so a slow plan cannot ride a shared directory into an edit it never reads ; a layered plan stays a named target but follows `--tier` like a directory, so the slow cases an ordinary change must not run (the PyTorch comparisons of autodiff and onnx) are filtered while the fast cases still run; `"layer": true` on the rule is the default for all its entries. A rule with "self": true selects the changed plan file itself (editing a plan runs that plan), except for the paths in "except": those fall back to the fast layer instead of running perf, GC stress, progen or PyTorch. A non-plan file under test/plans (a golden, a fixture) selects the nearest directory that holds a plan, so editing a golden runs the plans it belongs to. A change no rule matches (or whose plans cannot be found) falls back to the whole fast layer; `--changed --list` prints the selection without running it. The base branch is origin/develop; CAMEL_TEST_BASE overrides it. A tracked file that matches no rule is a hole, not a silent fallback: when a change also touches a file a rule matches, the unruled file contributes nothing. test/tools/selftest/run.mjs therefore fails on such a file unless it is on its allowlist, which names only the classes the project forbids (perf, GC stress, progen, PyTorch) or that no plan reads (vendored code, packaging, CI configuration). Deliberately not selectable: test/plans/perf/**, the GC-stress plans (feat/mm/gc*, gpu/tiles_regions) and progen (feat/opt/progen.plan.toml) -- the project forbids those on a shared host, so a change there runs the fast layer and the report says so instead of wiring them in. The same self-test now checks the other direction too: every plan file under test/plans must be selected by at least one of the case paths it names, so a plan --changed can never reach cannot hide behind cases that select another plan; plans the policy keeps unselectable (perf, GC stress, progen, the debug layer) and a sweep-only plan are the only exemptions. Update this file when a subsystem grows a plan of its own; see docs/test-plans.md, 'Selecting plans from a change'.

directoryRules.comment: The graph-space gradient case is a fast mm case that lives in the GC directory: the generic test/cases rule below resolves that directory to feat/mm/gc.plan.toml, the slow GC-stress plan, which does not run it. This exact path comes first and names no fall-through, so the file rule for the case selects feat/mm/graph_space instead.

The process-state cases are fast mm cases that live in the GC directory: the generic test/cases rule below resolves that directory to feat/mm/gc.plan.toml, the slow GC-stress plan, which runs neither of them. These exact paths come first and name no fall-through, so a change to either selects the feat/mm directory (layered, so the slow plans there still follow --tier).

The context-lifetime case is a fast mm case that lives in the GC directory as well: the generic test/cases rule below resolves that directory to feat/mm/gc.plan.toml, the slow GC-stress plan, which does not run it. This exact path comes first and names no fall-through, so the file rule for the case selects the plan that reads it.

The formatted-print case is a fast consistency program that happens to live under the cpp exec dump directory: the generic test/cases rule below resolves it to feat/trans/cpp.plan.toml, whose agree_with_fvm test compiles and runs C++ for up to ten minutes, and which does not run this case. This exact path comes first and falls through to the file rule that names print_formats.

The seed corpus of the progen finding cases (test/cases/opt/progen/findings): no plan directory mirrors it, and the generic test/cases rule below would resolve it to test/plans/feat/opt/progen.plan.toml -- the slow random-program check an ordinary change must never run in full. This rule comes first and names no fall-through, so the directory rule selects nothing here and the file rule for those cases names progen_simplify instead.
The cases whose own path starts with feat/ (test/cases/feat/mm, ...): the generic rule below would look for test/plans/feat/feat/mm. This narrower match comes first, so mm cases select feat/mm.
A test case: its directory is looked up under test/plans/feat (compile, linear, modules/tensor, modules/nn.plan.toml, tools/unicode -> tools, ...).
A module: modules/tensor selects feat/modules/tensor, modules/nn selects feat/modules/nn.plan.toml. A module with no plan of its own (python) falls through to the file rules.
A tool: tools/lsp selects feat/tools/lsp.plan.toml; tools/format falls through to the file rules (feat/format).

rules.comment: The parse-check harness, the selftest fixtures and the load-class guard: a change here runs smoke, the runner plan, the load-class plan (its cases are the selftest fixtures) and the front-end plan (layered so its slow fuzz test is filtered under --tier fast).
The runner itself and the self-test: the plans that exercise the runner and the smoke set.
The debugger harness (the DAP race harness): the plan whose slow DAP cases it drives. A harness change is not a plan change, but this is the plan that would catch a regression in it.
The language-server test client.

The other test harnesses (cppexec, parsecheck, jitcov, progen, gcbench, ...): no plan tests a harness directly, and naming the plan that invokes one would mean naming most of feat/. The smallest honest check is smoke plus the runner plan, which is what a harness change can break first. The specific debugger and LSP clients above are narrower because their plans own them.
FastVM and the other schedulers.

The optimization passes and the rewrite rule library they run: the opt plans, the pass dumps that print their effect, the rewrite-rule plan, and feat/compile for the module registration and operator declarations a rewrite-module change can break. stdlib/rules.cml is the data these passes run, so it selects the same set. `feat/opt` is a directory target, so `--tier fast` keeps its fast plans and filters the slow progen plan (progen is never selected by a rule). The rule library's own SMT check is selected here too: it reads stdlib/rules.cml, so a rule that stops holding under its licence is reported by the change that edited it.
The profiler pass: its own plan runs without a CUDA device (the host fallback), so it is safe from an ordinary change.
The other translation passes: the graph printers, the C++ emitter, the JSON dump.
The test-only passes (test::facts, test::regions, test::rules, ...): the plans that name them in their arguments.
Any other pass, including the shared pass machinery.
GCT/GIR construction, encoding and the graph printer.
The front end: lexer, parser, AST and diagnostics.

Values, types, the collector and the runtime shell. The array type's dimensions live here, so its self-test runs too. The direct-connection ledger of graph-store step 2 b is checked here as well: its three numbers count the references to `GraphDraft`, and `src/runtime/` is where both the storage and the transaction live, so this is the directory a commit can add a direct connection from. The plan is fast and cheap (one `git grep` pass), so it rides along rather than waiting for its own gate.
Execution, entry arguments and the standalone bridge.

The rest of src/: the built-in operators and their semantic tables (src/builtin) are the core every module plan runs on, so feat/modules is included; the services, profiler helpers and utilities are reached through the compiler and the runtime. The specific rules above stay narrower.

The public headers mirror src/: a header a pass or the runtime includes is as wide as the source file that includes it. These rules mirror the src/ rules above, so a header change selects the same plans as the implementation it declares.
The compiler and graph headers.
The pass API headers: the translation, optimization and scheduler passes.

The core value/type headers and the runtime headers. The array type's dimensions live here, so its self-test runs too. The ledger's `files`/`references` count is partly a header count (`include/camel/runtime/draft.h`, `draft_session.h`, ...), so this rule names the ledger plan for the same reason the src/ one does.
The executor and entry-argument headers.
Any other public header (init, utils, services, the standalone bridge): the compiler, the translator and the runtime, which is the smallest set every consumer of include/ shares.

Tiles, the module: the CPU plan, the three GPU plans (all slow, so they are named as plan files and run in full even under --tier fast), the profile and reading plans, and the DDPM plan whose training cases are written against tiles. A module change can invalidate every consumer, and the GPU plans are what no directory rule could reach before.

A tiles case: the CPU plan is the directory mirror, and the DDPM, profile and reading plans read some of these cases. The three GPU plans are slow (88 tests) and are added only for the cases they name (`ownCases`): a case edit cannot invalidate a GPU plan that does not run it, which is what kept a one-case edit running a whole GPU plan in full. The GPU plan that shares a case with a fast plan is recorded in `slowCaseOwners`.

The ONNX exporter. `layer` is true because the plan's four slow cases are ONNX Runtime and PyTorch comparisons: under --tier fast the fast exporter tests run and those are filtered; --tier all runs them. `feat/trans` holds the dumps that print the exported graph. `onnx_with_forms` pins the three call forms of `export_model`'s `with` list (only `out`; `out` with `target`; `out` with `dynamic_axes`), one case under `test/cases/modules/onnx/with_forms/` each.
Neural-network operators: the nn plan and the plans that train with them.
Automatic differentiation. `layer` is true because five slow cases compare gradients against PyTorch: --tier fast runs the fast autodiff cases and filters those.

Tensor operators and shapes: the tensor plans, the index/operator semantics plans, the thread budget (the pool and the library GEMM share one number), the numeric licence that the library path is allowed under, and autodiff (layered, for the same PyTorch reason), because a shape or operator change shows up in gradients.

Keyed random: the random plan, whose slow std::cpp comparison follows --tier (`layer`) so a change to a case does not run it in full, the reference plan that runs the Philox cases, and the registry that lists them.
Graph values and passes, and the rewrite rules built on them.
Checkpoint trees.
I/O: the module's plan and the std facade that wraps it.
JSON values: the accessor/typed/value plans and the std facade.
Bytes and the std facade over them.
Parallel operators: the para plans and the registry that lists their signatures.
The Python bridge: the std plan whose python cases run it and the two consistency plans that drive it.
Numeric operators: the std facade and the operator-semantics plan.
The declaration modules with no plan of their own: their cases live under test/cases/modules/std, which feat/modules/std.plan.toml runs, and their signatures are checked by the registry plan.
Any other module. A directory target, so --tier fast filters the slow cases; a module that grows a specific rule above stops using this one.

The computed halves of the declarations (stdlib/signatures/<module>.cml): they are not compiled; stdlib-reference.mjs --verify-ops compares them with the operators the module registers, and --verify-doc regenerates docs/stdlib-reference.md from them. That is exactly feat/modules/stdlib_registry, so this rule is narrower than the declaration-body rule below and comes first.

The declaration bodies (stdlib/<module>.cml): a declaration is compiled (feat/compile) and loaded at startup (smoke), it is imported by every module plan that uses its operators (feat/modules, a directory so --tier fast keeps the ProGen/GC/PyTorch entries out), and --verify-ops/--verify-doc check it against the registry. stdlib/rules.cml is matched by the optimizer rule above, which is narrower.
The std facade over the modules: the module plan that exercises it, the compile checks of its imports, and the registry that lists its operators.
The language server, debugger, formatter and command-line tools.
The documentation guards: docs_links runs the link and snippet checks.
The stdlib reference generator and the migration guard: stdlib_registry runs --verify-ops, --verify-doc and stdlib-declarations --check. The computed halves it reads are checked by the same plan.
The grammar generator/checker: parse.frontend's grammar.reference_in_step keeps the generated reference, the parser productions and the token/node tables in step.

The reference for AI readers and the script that generates its four regions from the token table, the parser productions, the diagnostics registry and the stdlib page: docs_ai_reference re-checks the regions, the diagnostic names and the character budget, and compiles every counter-example against the compiler; docs_links compiles and runs the page's snippets like any other reader-facing page.

The standard-include check: portability.std_includes runs it over src, include, modules and tools. The source-tree artifact check is the same kind of property of the sources, and portability.source_artifacts runs it. The checker's --clean delegates to scripts/clean.js, whose own plan pins the tiers and the tracked-file rule.

The diagnostics registry: compile.diag_catalog runs --check, the failure-path proof, --verify-doc and --coverage; the registry is the one declaration file and the generated tables live beside the code they number.
The header sweep: docs.headers runs headers.mjs --check over the tree, and --check --root over its own fixture (test/plans/feat/headers/fixture).

The plan inventory: feat/gate/plan_inventory runs scripts/plan-inventory.mjs -- the one implementation of the four fates a plan file can have and of the check that every plan file has one, which the release gate imports rather than restating. A new plan that lands without a fate must redden the commit that lands it, so this is the fast-layer entry for that check, and a change to the tables or the check selects it. The case ledger lives in the same module, and feat/gate/case_ledger is its own fast-layer entry: a case that lands with nothing that reads it must redden the commit that lands it, the same way.

The conformance matrix: gate.conformance runs the checker over the recorded readings, so a change to the checker, to the manifest or to a case must run that plan. The cases and the manifest live under test/conformance, outside test/cases, where no case directory rule reaches them.

The other build/dev scripts (build.js, format.js, collect-out.js, ...): every plan runs the binary they build, but no plan reads them. Smoke is the smallest check that the toolchain still produces a working camel. scripts/perf-gate.mjs is covered here too: smoke does not run a perf plan.
The showcase's training step: the plan runs the naive Transformer example on the three CPU back ends and pins the fixed-seed losses.

The MCTS showcase: showcase/d4-mcts/search.cml is pinned by a fast plan (the whole standard output of four searches on four back ends, the properties that move if the search is wrong, and three refusals), so an edit to the example runs it. The directory's perf case (compare.py, the Camel/Python comparison) stays where the perf layer keeps it, unselectable by an ordinary change; the other showcase directories remain on the rule-less allowlist, which is why `showcase/` is still listed there.

The diffusion training step (I2's CPU precursor): showcase/i2-diffusion-step/step.cml is pinned by a fast plan (the whole standard output of three DDPM steps at a stated seed, on the default back end and std::prl, plus the property that the loss falls), so an edit to the example runs it. The other showcase directories remain on the rule-less allowlist, which is why `showcase/` is still listed there.

The stream showcase: showcase/s1-stream-fib/fib.cml is pinned by a fast plan (the whole standard output -- the ten Fibonacci numbers below 50 and their sum, 88 -- on the default back end and std::prl, plus the properties that the sequence is Fibonacci and that the total is the sum of the elements), so an edit to the example runs it. The other showcase directories remain on the rule-less allowlist, which is why `showcase/` is still listed there.
Example programs and their recorded output.
The CPython binding of the runtime: the extension module links libcamel and is read by the Python binding plan, which drives it from an interpreter (the test skips where the extension was not built).
The exemplars and their checker: feat/exemplars re-runs every exemplar and checks its recorded output.

The chapter examples beside the tutorial (docs/tutorial/examples/*.cml): the plan that runs each of them as a file and pins what it prints, plus the documentation check, because a page links to the file it shows and a rename or a deletion breaks that link, plus the picture check, because a picture is drawn from the example beside it. This rule is narrower than the general docs rule and comes before it, so a tutorial page itself still selects that rule.

The tool that draws the tutorial's pictures and the pictures themselves: docs.tutorial_images re-dumps every example its sheet names and requires images/<name>.dot to be what comes out, so an edit to the tool or to a picture has to run it. It draws nothing -- the comparison is of DOT, and the redraw needs Graphviz -- so it rides the fast layer.
The generated stdlib reference: stdlib_registry.registry.reference_is_generated re-runs --verify-doc, so a hand edit fails there; docs_links is the ordinary documentation check.
The generated diagnostics catalog: compile.diag_catalog.catalog.doc_is_generated re-runs --verify-doc.
A design page and its sources are edited together; a design change selects the documentation checks the general docs rule runs.

Documentation checks. The root Markdown files are scanned by the same guards (README, CONTRIBUTING, ROADMAP, the code of conduct); agents/ is the development guide. llms.txt is the root index of the reference for AI readers, so a change to it is a documentation change. Smoke is included because a documentation change is usually part of a code change and the report's gate runs it; it is ten tests, not a mirror of the tree.
Images the documents link to: docs_links checks that a relative link's target file exists, so adding or removing an asset is a documentation-link change. Images have no plan of their own.
The editor syntax files and their tests.
The build definitions: every backend may be affected, so the smoke set and the runtime plans.
The graph-space gradient case: the directory rule above keeps the slow GC plan off it, and this is the fast plan that runs it.
The process-state cases: the directory rule above keeps the slow GC plan off them, and this is the fast plan that runs them.
The context-lifetime case: the directory rule above keeps the slow GC plan off it, and this is the fast plan that runs it.
The smoke cases: test/plans/smoke is outside the feat/ tree, so no directory rule can mirror test/cases/smoke.

The resource-surface cases (`resource`/`unordered`, `#resource` on a nominal type, `uses`/`pure` on a declaration or a function type): they are front-end/compile cases, and their plan is a file under feat/compile with no `test/plans/feat/effects` directory to mirror the case directory, so the generic test/cases directory rule resolves them to nothing. Name the one plan that reads them. The runtime plans (feat/modules, feat/tools, feat/trans) do not read these cases, so they are not added.

A case directory with no plan directory of its own: the loop cases are tested by the linear loop plans. loops.plan.toml is not the only one: hof_declared (higher-order declarations), loops_in_arms and loop_collect each name cases in this directory, and a change to those cases has no other rule to select them.
The macro cases: the definitions/facts/resources group below also covers them, plus the linear plan whose higher-order declaration cases live here.
Case directories with no plan directory of their own: their cases are exercised by the module, tool and translation plans.

The JSON cases: they live in one directory that no plan directory mirrors (the JSON plans are files under feat/modules). A JSON case change can break any of the three JSON plans and the std facade that wraps them, and none of those cases selects its plan otherwise.
The unicode-path case: its plan lives under feat/modules, and the generic test/cases rule resolves this directory only as far as the feat/tools directory. Name the plan that runs the case.

The formatted-print case is shared by the consistency plan and the cpp dumps, but its own directory resolves to feat/trans/cpp.plan.toml, which does not run print_formats: name the plan whose test it is.

The tuple-expansion program whose splice refuses to move a statement: its own directory resolves to feat/compile/static_expansion.plan.toml, which does not run opt.sync_chain, so that plan would be one --changed can never reach. Name the plan whose test it is.

The three programs the splice left forked: their own directories resolve to feat/consistency, feat/compile/stream and feat/linear, none of which runs opt.splice_place. Name the plan whose tests they are.

The compiler benchmark's smoke test (benchmarks/compile/bench.py) is feat/tools/compile_bench: a change to its case must select the plan that runs it. The rest of benchmarks/ stays the manual perf layer, as the rule-less allowlist says.

The progen finding cases are the seed corpus of progen_simplify (fast) and capacity (fast), not of the progen plan itself: the directory-rule exception above keeps them from naming progen, and these are the plans that read them. capacity runs only `const_graph_capacity.cml` in that corpus, so it is named by ownership (`ownCases`) rather than by the whole directory.

The judgement programs are the corpus of open design questions: the cpp harness reads one of them through test/tools/cppexec/expect.txt, and the translation plan runs that harness. The README and the findings index are documentation of the manual progen tool and are on the self-test's rule-less allowlist.

A plan file selects itself: editing the tests of one plan runs that plan. A non-plan file under test/plans (a golden, a fixture) selects the nearest directory that holds a plan, so editing a golden runs the plans it belongs to. The except list keeps the plans the project forbids from an ordinary change out of that: a perf, GC-stress or progen plan edit falls back to the fast layer (name the plan file to run it deliberately).

slowCaseOwners.comment: Slow plans whose cases live in a directory a fast plan also uses. `ownCases` already keeps such a plan off the cases it does not run; this list records the cases it does run that a fast plan also runs, where the slow plan is therefore not the only owner of the changed path. The reason says why the slow plan must still run. The self-test derives the facts: it requires every entry to be a slow-cost plan (tier slow, a slow test, or a timeout of five minutes or more) that names at least one case a fast plan also names, so an entry that excuses nothing fails.

entries.why: Its GPU tests share resident.cml with the fast screens plan: a case that a fast and a slow plan both exercise can break only on one of them, so the case edit must run both. The plan stays slow because it needs a CUDA device and its 83 tests take minutes.
